clinicalPearls: Mycoplasma genitalium is a small, slow-growing, cell-wall-deficient bacterium and an established sexually transmitted cause of non-gonococcal urethritis in men and cervicitis in women
Many infections are asymptomatic; when symptomatic, men typically report dysuria and urethral discharge while women may have discharge, intermenstrual or postcoital bleeding, or pelvic pain
It is an important cause of persistent or recurrent non-gonococcal urethritis after treatment for presumed chlamydia and is linked to cervicitis and pelvic inflammatory disease
Diagnosis relies on nucleic acid amplification testing because the organism is extremely difficult to culture; lacking a cell wall, it is not seen on Gram stain
Wherever possible, positive samples should undergo testing for macrolide-resistance-mediating mutations to guide therapy, given rapidly rising macrolide resistance
First-line treatment is often azithromycin (frequently as an extended regimen) in macrolide-susceptible infection, with doxycycline commonly used to lower bacterial load beforehand
Moxifloxacin is reserved for macrolide-resistant or persistent infection, and treatment failure with escalating resistance is an increasing problem
Test of cure and partner notification are recommended, and routine screening of asymptomatic people is discouraged to limit resistance selection
reference.pathophysiology: Mycoplasma genitalium is among the smallest self-replicating bacteria and lacks a rigid cell wall, which renders it invisible on Gram stain and intrinsically resistant to cell-wall-active antibiotics such as beta-lactams. It is transmitted sexually and attaches to and glides along genital and urethral epithelial surfaces by means of a specialised terminal adhesion organelle, provoking a local inflammatory response that manifests as urethritis, cervicitis, or endometrial and tubal inflammation. Because it grows slowly and fastidiously, infection tends to be indolent and persistent, and its capacity to acquire mutations in the 23S ribosomal RNA gene (conferring macrolide resistance) and in topoisomerase genes (conferring fluoroquinolone resistance) underlies the growing difficulty in achieving cure.
additionalDifferentials: Ureaplasma or other genital mollicute infection
additionalInvestigations: Nucleic acid amplification testing of first-void urine (men) or vaginal, endocervical, or urine samples (women)
Reflex molecular testing for 23S rRNA macrolide-resistance mutations on positive specimens
Concurrent nucleic acid amplification testing for chlamydia and gonorrhoea
Microscopy of urethral or genital smears to document urethritis or cervicitis where available
Test of cure by nucleic acid amplification testing several weeks after completing treatment
Screening for other sexually transmitted infections including HIV and syphilis
redFlags: Features of pelvic inflammatory disease such as pelvic pain, adnexal tenderness, or fever
Persistent or recurrent urethritis despite appropriate first-line therapy suggesting antimicrobial resistance
Repeated treatment failure indicating multidrug-resistant infection needing specialist input
reference.prognosis: Susceptible infections usually respond to appropriate antibiotics, but rising macrolide and emerging fluoroquinolone resistance make persistent and recurrent infection increasingly common; untreated or inadequately treated disease may contribute to pelvic inflammatory disease and associated reproductive sequelae.
pitfalls: Treating with azithromycin without resistance-guided testing, which can select for macrolide resistance
Assuming persistent non-gonococcal urethritis is chlamydia and not testing for Mycoplasma genitalium
Screening asymptomatic individuals, which drives unnecessary treatment and resistance
Omitting test of cure and partner notification, allowing reinfection and onward transmission
